newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Head of Ecuadorean military rejects Peru landmine charge.
newsitem.headline: Head of Ecuadorean military rejects Peru landmine charge.

text.p: The head of Ecuador's armed forces has rejected a Peruvian charge that captured Ecuadorean troops were caught laying mines in a jungle border zone which sparked a month-long war in 1995.

"I have read the press reports that the soldiers were carrying 600 landmines -- that's something you can't believe. How can seven men walk seven kilometres (four miles) with 600 landmines?" General Paco Moncayo, head of Ecuador's joint chiefs of staff, told local television late on Wednesday.
But Moncayo admitted the Ecuadorean patrol captured by Peru might have strayed into undisputed Peruvian territory.
"I am not ruling anything out. That could have happened," he said. "You have to understand that it was a routine mission in which that can happen."
Moncayo said Ecuadorean and Peruvian troops often cross over into each others territory along the jungle frontier.

The Peruvian army said on Wednesday that it captured a heavily armed seven-strong Ecuadorean army patrol weighed down with 600 antipersonnel mines, and that the soldiers had admitted they had been ordered to lay the mines.
Moncayo said that there was no fighting in the incident and that no one was hurt. He said that the Ecuadorean authorities had ordered an investigation.

"We are worried by what has happened. We regret that this incident should have occurred just when our delegations are negotiating peace but I do not believe that it should be any reason at all for causing problems in the negotiations," he said.
The incident came as Ecuadorean and Peruvian officials were set to start a second round of talks on their border disputes in Brasilia.
Peru said the captured men would be handed over to Ecuador on Thursday by an international peace mission, known by its Spanish initials MOMEP, which monitors compliance of a provisional peace treaty.
Ecuador's Defence Ministry said on Wednesday that the patrol was carrying out its normal duties and that Ecuador would lodge complaints through diplomatic channels.

The two countries fought a month-long war in January 1995 over a stretch of their jungle border. Dozens of soldiers were killed and hundreds injured from both sides in the fighting, which followed a long border dispute.
